title: Second sign: ancient liturgies prayed for all the dead, even apostles and the Virgin
source_text: LXII. Deinde ex vetustissimis quae supersunt Liturgiis constat, veteres illos Christianos obtulisse Deo preces & supplicationes pro omnibus omnino mortuis, etiam pro Sanctissimis, pro Martyribus, pro Apostolis, adeoque pro ipsa Deipara Virgine. Pro quibus a Deo petunt in Liturgiis illis ut eos requiescere faciat in regione viventium, & largiatur iis promissionum suarum bona, & praestet requiem bonamque memoriam: non vero, simpliciter, ut frustra contendit Bellarminus, pro iis gratiarum actiones offerunt. Jam vero ex quo publice receptus est Religiosus Sanctorum cultus & invocatio, tanquam oraculum illud Augustini habitum est, Injuriam facere Martyri qui orat pro Martyre. Nec unquam aliquis in animum inducet ut utatur solenni illa invocatione, quam Sanctis cum Christo regnantibus deberi docet Ecclesia Romana, apud eos quos opus sit precibus nostris Deo commendari.
pass_a_gloss: Then from the most ancient Liturgies which survive it is established that those ancient Christians offered to God prayers and supplications for absolutely all the dead, even for the most Holy, for the Martyrs, for the Apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. For whom they ask from God in those Liturgies that he make them rest in the region of the living, and bestow on them the goods of his promises, and grant rest and good memory: and not, simply, as Bellarmine vainly contends, do they offer thanksgivings for them. But now since the Religious worship and invocation of the Saints was publicly received, that oracle of Augustine has been held as it were, He does injury to a Martyr who prays for a Martyr. Nor will anyone ever bring his mind to use that solemn invocation, which the Roman Church teaches is owed to the Saints reigning with Christ, toward those whom it is needful to commend to God by our prayers.
pass_b_english: Second, the oldest surviving liturgies show that those early Christians offered prayers and supplications to God for absolutely all the dead, even for the holiest, for the martyrs, for the apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. In those liturgies they ask God to give them rest in the land of the living, to grant them the good things he has promised, and to give them rest and a good remembrance. They are not simply offering thanks for them, as Bellarmine vainly argues.

But ever since the religious worship and invocation of the saints was publicly received, Augustine's saying has been treated almost as an oracle: "He wrongs a martyr who prays for a martyr." And no one will ever bring himself to use the solemn invocation that the Roman Church teaches is owed to the saints reigning with Christ toward people who need to be commended to God by our prayers.
